extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (especially aesthetics, epistemology, and Kantian studies)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Immanuel Kant's standards for aesthetic and reflective judgement as presented in the Critique of Judgement: distinctions between determinant/reflective judgement, the transcendental principle of purposiveness, and the relation of feeling (pleasure/pain) to cognitive faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetical Judgement: reference to feeling of pleasure or pain a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetical judgements concern the Beautiful and the Sublime of Nature or of Art and 'point to an immediate reference of this faculty to the feeling of pleasure or pain according to some principle a priori.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such judgements do not by themselves add to knowledge of things but belong to the cognitive faculty; they must be understood as referring immediately to a feeling (pleasure/pain) grounded by a principle that is a priori. They are to be treated distinct from principles that determine the faculty of desire (practical Reason).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant vs. Reflective Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement is the faculty of thinking the particular as contained under the Universal. If the universal is given, judgement that subsumes the particular is 'determinant'; if only the particular is given and the universal must be found, the judgement is 'reflective.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'determinant' when subsumption under an already-given transcendental law is possible (no search for law needed). Use 'reflective' where one must ascend from particulars to seek a principle or unity—reflective judgement requires supplying a principle from itself and cannot borrow it from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the (Formal) Purposiveness of Nature (transcendental principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle for reflective judgement is the purposiveness of nature in its manifoldness: 'nature is represented by means of this concept, as if an Understanding contained the ground of the unity of the manifold of its empirical laws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat purposiveness as a transcendental (a priori) principle that guides reflection about empirical laws: we must represent empirical variety as if organized by an Understanding so that a systematic experience is possible. This principle is a law of reflection (subjective a priori), not an objective law imposed on nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish transcendental vs. metaphysical purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: A transcendental principle represents a priori the universal condition under which things can be objects of cognition; a principle is metaphysical if it represents an a priori condition under which objects (whose concept must be empirically given) can be further determined a priori. The principle of formal purposiveness of nature is transcendental; practical purposiveness (in the Idea of determination of a free will) is metaphysical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about purposiveness, identify whether the claim is a transcendental condition for cognition (concerned with possibility of experience) or a metaphysical claim that presupposes empirical concepts (e.g., faculties of desire). Do not conflate practical purposiveness (morals/art) with the formal purposiveness used in reflective judgement about nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Specification of Nature (a priori maxim for Judgement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judgement prescribes to itself an a priori law for reflection: a 'law of the specification of nature in respect of its empirical laws' — i.e., even where particulars are contingent, reflection assumes a specifiable order amenable to systematisation by the Understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In reflective work one must assume (for the sake of inquiry) that particular empirical laws can be arranged under a unity that makes systematic experience possible. This is not a claim about nature itself but a methodological presupposition of coherent investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality/Communicability of the Feeling of Pleasure in Aesthetic Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The attainment of the Understanding's design (unity of principles) is bound up with the feeling of pleasure; since the condition of this attainment is a representation a priori, 'the feeling of pleasure is determined by a ground a priori and valid for every man' by reference of the object to the cognitive faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming an aesthetic judgement, one appeals to a feeling whose validity is presented as universally communicable: judgement of taste relies on the idea that the pleasure taken in purposive form is not merely private but has a claim to validity for all, grounded in the relation between object and cognitive faculties (not in desire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxims for reflective Judgement (methodological heuristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scattered maxims guide reflective judgement about nature: e.g., 'Nature takes the shortest way (lex parsimoniae); at the same time it makes no leaps (lex continui in natura); its great variety in empirical laws is yet unity under a few principles (principia praeter necessitatem non sunt multiplicanda),' etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these maxims as methodological heuristics when seeking systematic unity in empirical diversity—favor parsimonious explanations, continuity, and the hypothesis that diversity may fall under few unifying principles. These are not empirical demonstrations but regulative maxims for reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement as intermediary between Understanding and Reason (faculties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement is a middle faculty between the Understanding (faculty of knowledge) and the Reason (faculty of desire/practical reason); it may contain a special principle (merely subjective a priori) that mediates from cognition to the realm of freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing philosophical problems, recognise the mediating role of judgement: it enables transitions (e.g., from theoretical cognition to practical ideas) and thus must be treated as having its own principles and limits. Do not mistake its subjective a priori maxims for objective laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to assume a unity of empirical laws for the possibility of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: For the possibility of a connected experience, the Judgement must presuppose that particular empirical laws, though contingent in our insight, contain a unity of law in their combination; otherwise no systematic experience or investigation is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating natural phenomena or constructing systematic accounts, assume (as a regulative principle) that empirical plurality can be integrated into a coherent system. This assumption is a necessary presupposition for the enterprise of inquiry, not an empirical proof about nature itself.
